slides.about: Title, a Breaking Camp housekeeping slide for your announcements, the Skill Spotlight, group roles, 16Personalities with a QR code, collaboration strategies, the AI group-plan Trail Tip, this week's work (including Merit Activity #3), Mile Marker #10, and an in-class discussion. Every slide has a talk track in the speaker notes, so the deck also works as a script for an online mini-lecture.

coaching.head: Group work stories come with feelings.
coaching.body: Many students carry a bad group project story. Let them tell it, but keep it to roles, not names, and steer toward what would have helped.

coaching.head: Question 1: own words, not the official description.
coaching.body: Students sometimes paste the 16Personalities description. The question asks for one short phrase in their own words, plus strengths and challenges that honestly fit.

coaching.head: Question 2 is a tendency, not a flaw.
coaching.body: Students explain why one challenge happens. Some will mention neurodivergence; sharing it is always optional. Respond to the insight, not the label.

coaching.head: Question 3 should be one sentence.
coaching.body: "I need teammates to tell me early if plans change" is the target: simple, respectful, and specific.

coaching.head: Merit #3 is the last one.
coaching.body: Students who are behind on Merit run out of time here. Check who still needs an activity early in the week, and point online students to a virtual meet-up.

coaching.head: 16Personalities isn't a diagnosis.
coaching.body: Treat the type as a map, not a rulebook. If a student feels boxed in by their result, that's worth naming in feedback.

meetup.topic: What this semester has taught you so far
meetup.why: It warms students up for the STAR(T) Stories in Modules 11 and 12.

activities.title: Role corners
activities.materials: The seven group roles from Lesson 10.2 posted around the room
steps: Students stand by the role that sounds most like them.
Each group names one thing their role brings and one way it frustrates other roles.
Students move to their second role and compare.
activities.why: Makes group differences visible and normal before students write about their own.
activities.online: Ask students to name their top two roles in the discussion.

activities.title: Set the expectations
steps: Groups answer the four questions from Lesson 10.5: the task, the deadlines, who's doing what, and what done looks like.
Each group writes one group norm.
Debrief: which question would have saved their worst group project?
activities.why: Practices the strategy that prevents most group conflict.
activities.online: Share the four questions in your announcement as a template for any group project.

activities.title: AI group plan, checked
activities.materials: A sample group assignment and an AI tool, if the assignment rules allow it
steps: Generate a task list and timeline with AI using the Trail Tip's steps.
Groups mark what AI got wrong or couldn't know, like who works evenings.
activities.why: Shows both the usefulness and the limits of AI for planning, and reinforces BE Responsible.
activities.online: Demonstrate the Trail Tip in your recorded mini-lecture.

discussion.title: When group work went sideways
prompt: Tell one group work story: good, bad, or somewhere in between. What went sideways?
What would have helped? Does your 16Personalities type explain any of it?
discussion.format: No names. Talk with a partner for 3 minutes, then share what would have helped.
discussion.source: An in-class version of the online discussion: That One Time Group Work Went Sideways. In-person students bring a story and their type.
discussion.facilitate: Set the no-names ground rule first. Collect what would have helped; most answers map to Lesson 10.5, especially clear expectations.
